title.official: Consolidation or separation of claims and actions

subdivision.heading: Joining and Separating Claims and Parties

operative_text.controlling:
3.72(1)  The Court may order one or more of the following:
(a) that 2 or more claims or actions be consolidated;
(b) that 2 or more claims or actions be tried at the same time
or one after the other;
(c) that one or more claims or actions be stayed until another
claim or action is determined;
(d) that a claim be asserted as a counterclaim in another
action.
(2)  An order under subrule (1) may be made for any reason the
Court considers appropriate, including, without limitation, that 2 or
more claims or actions
(a) have a common question of law or fact, or
(b) arise out of the same transaction or occurrence or series of
transactions or occurrences.

commentary.text: Rule 3.72 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.72. 1. General Rule for Joinder In Klychak v. Samchuk, 2012 ABQB 85, 2012 CarswellAlta 118, 532 A.R. 259; additional reasons 2012 ABQB 314, 2012 CarswellAlta 867, Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 38-39: 38 Rules 3.72 and 1.4(1) and s. 8 of the Judicature Act outline the Court's authority to order actions to be tried at the same time or one after the other. Case law, including Valerio and Mikisew, outline the types of factors which a court should consider when deciding whether to exercise its power under the Rules and the statute; although individual factors should be considered, the court's overall objective is to ensure that its decision on how the actions should be tried will serve the ends of justice: Alliance Pipeline. 39 Much of the case law cited by the parties was developed under the former Rules of Court; because of the similarity between the old Rules and the current ones, the existing case law continues to be applicable. Indeed, Rule 1.4 emphasizes the need to foster just and fair resolutions of disputes in a timely and cost-effective way. In Munro v. Munro, 2011 ABCA 279, 2011 CarswellAlta 1670, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 247, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 421, 2 R.F.L. (7th) 298, 341 D.L.R. (4th) 635, 513 A.R. 363, 530 W.A.C. 363, the husband appealed the dismissal of his application for an order to consolidate an action for breach of a matrimonial property agreement and an application for retroactive child support. At paragraphs 6-7, Justices Paperny and Bielby said: 6 An order to consolidate is discretionary, and the standard of review is reasonableness: Alliance Pipeline Limited v. Universal Ensco, Inc, 2007 ABCA 285 at para. 3; 417 AR 1. Absent a material error in principle, a significant misapprehension or disregard of the evidence, or a decision which is clearly wrong, an appellate court will not interfere with an exercise of discretion: AB v. CD, 2008 ABCA 51 at para. 10; 85 Alta LR (4th) 18. 7 When faced with an application to consolidate claims, a court must weigh several relevant factors. They include the extent to which there are common claims and disputes, and the possibility that consolidation may save time and resources in pre-trial procedures and at trial. The court must also consider potential prejudice to the parties which may arise from consolidation if, for example, one action is more advanced than the other and if consolidation will result in prejudicial delay of a trial. Master Smart, in Wong v. Leung, 2011 ABQB 722, 2011 CarswellAlta 2052, 530 A.R. 91 (Master), adopted that test (at paragraph 24). See also: AutoCanada Capital Motors GP Inc v. Mirbach, 2021 ABQB 170, 2021 CarswellAlta 474 at para. 6. In Center Street Limited Partnership v. Lloyd's Underwriters, 2017 ABQB 295, 2017 CarswellAlta 734, 50 Alta. L.R. (6th) 217 (Master), Master Robertson said: 12 The guiding principles in considering whether two or more cases should be consolidated or tried together were set out succinctly by the Court of Appeal in Alliance Pipeline Limited v C.E. Franklin Ltd, 2007 ABCA 285 at para. 6: The purpose of consolidation is to enhance the administration of justice. A court should consider the possibility of inconsistent verdicts, the prospect of prejudice to the parties and the impact of consolidation and non-consolidation, both at the pre-trial and trial stages on scarce resources, including administrative, judicial and financial. In other words, a court must be able to conclude that having regard to all the circumstances, on balance, it is in the interests of justice that the actions be consolidated. Some of the relevant factors that should be considered are discussed in Mikisew[cited below]. These, however, are not necessarily the only relevant factors, nor are they in themselves determinative. Each case must be assessed on its own merits and should include consideration, not just of the common claims, but the extent of the distinct claims between the parties. The focus in each case must be on the impact of consolidation on the parties and on the administration of justice. See also Anokhina v. Banovic, 2019 ABQB 774, 2019 CarswellAlta 2093 (paragraphs 20–23) for a summary of the law by Justice Lema. The following cases were decided under the previous Rules: Broadly speaking, where claims by or against different parties involve or may involve a common question of law or fact bearing sufficient importance in proportion to the rest of the action to render it desirable that the whole of the matters should be disposed of at the same time the Court will allow the joinder of plaintiffs or defendants, subject to its discretion as to how the action should be tried. Edmonton (City) v. Dominion Stores Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 677 (Alta. C.A.), at 680, per Ford C.J.A., quoting with approval Payne v. British Time Recorder Co., [1921] 2 K.B. 1 at 16. 2. When to Apply An application to split the action should be left to the trial judge. We have in the instant case a common question or questions of law in the different causes of action alleged against the different defendants, and this question, or questions as they may be, are fundamental to the success or failure of the entire action. True, the law may not be applicable in the same way to the different facts alleged in respect of each transaction, but that is for the trial Judge to decide …Edmonton (City) v. Dominion Stores Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 677 at 681 (Alta. C.A.). 3. Generally The general principle relating to the granting of a consolidation order is that the issues in both actions are identical… The underlying principle of R. 229 is to prevent the waste of resources by needless litigation. Welco Expediting Ltd. v. Harris (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 173 (Q.B.), at 187, per Moshansky J. And Medhurst J. said: There is provision in R. 229 of the Rules of Court for the consolidation of actions that (a) have a common question of law or fact, or (b) arise out of the same transaction or series of transactions. (See also R. 36 re joinder of causes of action). It is also stated in s. 32(k) [am. 1978, c. 51, s. 28] of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 193 that “as far as possible all matters in controversy between the parties [can] be completely determined and all multiplicity of legal proceedings concerning any such matters avoided.” The effect of consolidation is to combine two or more actions so that thereafter they will proceed as one action. One of the principal purposes of consolidation is to save expense and to avoid multiplicity of pleadings and proceedings. In Flitney v. Howard, [1958] O.R. 701 (C.A.), Morden J.A. observed that this purpose would only be accomplished if such an order were made at a very early stage and it would not be accomplished if granted on the eve of the trial. Scheidl v. Southam Inc. (1981), 16 Alta. L.R. (2d) 158 at 161 (Q.B.). This decision was reversed in result by the Court of Appeal [unreported] but the proposition was not criticized. See Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. (1984), 55 A.R. 44 (Master), at 45, for a note of the appeal proceedings. In Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. Master Funduk continued: 5. Rule 229 is not restricted to situations falling within items (a) or (b). There is a third catch all category, being “where for any other reason it is desirable to make an order under this Rule”. In Norwester Ltd. v. British Aviation Insurance Company Limited, 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 133 (N.W.T.S.C.), Tallis, J., indicates that there are two types of orders than can be granted at the same time, being an order that the actions be consolidated and an order that the actions be tried together. He indicates that in the second case that: 2. The actions may be ordered to be tried together. They are then set down on the list one after the other to be tried in such manner as the court directs. The trial judge has a discretion to direct that the evidence in one action is to be taken as evidence in the other action or actions. Nevertheless the actions maintain their separate identity and there are separate pleadings, discoveries, judgments and bills of costs. If the actions are tried together they are tried concurrently. In my view there is a third type of order, being that the actions be tried one after the other. In that case the actions are tried consecutively. In Giberson v. Labatt Breweries of British Columbia, [1980] 1 W.W.R. 93, (B.C. S.C.), Legg, J., ordered two actions to be tried at the same time. He states, at p. 96: In the case at bar it is apparent from the pleadings that all the facts and circumstances giving rise to the event which caused the plaintiff's injury will be canvassed before the trial judge in the first action. It therefore appears reasonable that the same trial judge should determine the question of whether the defendant solicitors are liable in the second action at the same time. It is submitted, however, that the defendant solicitors should not be put to the inconvenience and expense of attending at the trial of the first action if a consolidation is ordered or of awaiting the outcome of the first action if it is ordered that the two actions be tried at the same time or on the same day. Against this there is the convenience of the plaintiff in seeking to have all her causes of action arising out of the circumstances which gave rise to both actions adjudicated by the same trial judge and, if possible, on the same general occasion of trial. On appeal, reported, [1980] 2 W.W.R. 689 (C.A.), was dismissed. McFarlane, J.A., for the court, states at p. 689: I point out that the trial judge did not order these actions consolidated; neither did he unequivocally direct that they be tried at the same time, in the sense that all of the evidence in the one case would be evidence in the other. His reasons for judgment, the effect of which is carried into the formal order, provide that the two actions be tried at the same time or on the same day and with all subject to the discretion of the trial judge. I think the possible objections which have been raised as grounds of appeal are matters properly to be taken into consideration by the judge before whom these two actions come to be tried, and I see no basis upon which this court would be justified in allowing the appeal. Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. (1984), 55 A.R. 44 at 46-47 (Master). Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. was approved in Henuset Brothers Ltd. v. I.U.O.E., Local 955 (1984), 57 A.R. 258 at 265 (Q.B.). Moore C.J.Q.B., in Northland Bank v. Willson (1997), 56 Alta. L.R. (3d) 130 (Q.B.), at p. 135, said the following about the purpose of the rule: In Reichmann v. Toronto Life Publishing Co. (No. 1) (1988), 31 C.P.C. (2d) 54 (Ont. S.C.), the court held that the overriding purpose of the rules consolidating matters is to secure the just determination of the matters in dispute by assessing the balance of convenience to the plaintiffs and defendants. Moore J., in Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1998), 224 A.R. 157 (Q.B.), set forth factors that should be considered in an application to consolidate actions. At p. 158, His Lordship said: In Shah v. Bakkenn (1996), 46 C.P.C. (3d) 205 (B.C. C.A.) (sic; the Shah decision was a decision of Master Joyce of the B.C.S.C.), the court lists a number of factors which [one] should take into account in an application to consolidate. These include: i) whether there are common claims, disputes and relationships between the parties; ii) whether consolidation will save time and resources in pretrial procedures; iii) whether time at trial will be reduced; iv) whether one party will be seriously prejudiced by having two trials together; v) whether one action is at a more advanced stage than the other; and vi) whether consolidation will delay the trial of one action which will cause serious prejudice to one party. Kent J., in Andy & Jean Grebely Holdings Ltd. v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. of Canada, 2000 ABQB 604, 2000 CarswellAlta 958, (sub nom. Grebely v. Economical Mutual Insurance Co., 282 A.R. 296, agreed that the above noted factors are the ones to be considered in an old rule 229 (current rule 3.72) application (see p. 299). Justice Kenny, in Frydman v. Pelletier, 2013 ABQB 225, 2013 CarswellAlta 495, 559 A.R. 388, said, at paragraph 40: 40 The court maintains discretion as to when it is appropriate to consolidate actions under Rule 3.72. Some factors to consider are set out in Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1998), 224 AR 157 (QB) at p 158. These are: a) whether there are common claims, disputes, and relationships between the parties; b) whether consolidation will save time and resources in pretrial procedures; c) whether time at trial will be reduced; d) whether one party will be seriously prejudiced by having two trials together; e) whether one action is at a more advanced stage than the other; and f) whether consolidation will delay the trial of one action which will cause serious prejudice to one party. 4. Onus In Meyer v. Altex Energy Ltd., 2019 ABQB 787, 2019 CarswellAlta 2365, Justice Woolley discussed the onus borne by the party seeking consolidation of actions: [15] I also reject the Respondents' position that the Applicants bear a “heavy onus” in relation to consolidation. The Respondents cite jurisprudence from the Federal Court which states that the onus is on the party seeking consolidation to prove that the respondent parties would not suffer applicable prejudice or injustice: Sanofi-Aventis Canada Inc v Novopharm Ltd 2009 FC 1285 at para 11. In some cases the Federal Court has described this as a “heavy onus”: Mon-Oil Ltd v R (1989) 47 FTR 50 cited in Sanofi-Aventis at para 12. [16] I agree that the Applicants bear the onus of showing that consolidation is appropriate. But that onus is not “heavy.” It is neither heavy nor light; it is simply an onus to show on the balance of probabilities that this matter is an appropriate one for consolidation in accordance with Rule 3.72 and the governing jurisprudence. I note in this respect that the test for consolidation concerns the administration of justice and conserving judicial resources and, significantly, that wasting judicial resources puts access to justice at risk. The interests at stake in a consolidation application are not merely those of the parties, but take into account the broader community who seek access to the court system. As a judge of this court I am obligated to protect the administration of justice and to ensure the proper use of judicial and other resources, and my consideration of those matters ought not to be limited through imposing an unusual or undue onus on an applicant. 5. Order Should Not Be Granted if it Will Delay Litigation In Ellis-Don Management Services v. Rae-Dawn Construction Ltd. (1992), 131 A.R. 190 (C.A.), the court considered an order which directed that certain construction lawsuits could not be tried until judgment was rendered in related insurance proceedings. The construction lawsuits were advancing at a slower pace than the other matters. The Court of Appeal, speaking through Côté J.A., set aside the order and, at p. 191, said: It is desirable to try to do something to avoid duplication of proceedings or inconsistent verdicts. But in our view that cannot always be done, and should not be done where it unfairly retards litigation. 6. Consolidation versus Trials at Same Time In my view the allegations in these two actions fall squarely within the requirements of Rule 229. However, I do not think it is in the best interests of the parties that the two actions be consolidated for trial for, as I understand the effect of this type of order, it would make one action out of the two and create a great deal of confusion as to who are plaintiffs, defendants and plaintiffs and defendants by counterclaim. Rule 229 also provides that the court can order that the actions be tried at the same time and this seems to me to be far less cumbersome while achieving the desirable result of allowing a Trial Judge to hear all of the relevant matters without the necessity of two separate trials covering similar evidence and witnesses. Athabasca Realty Co. v. Humeniuk (1978), 14 A.R. 79 (T.D.), at 85, per Miller J. And Medhurst J. said: The alternate question to consider, however, is whether the two actions should be tried at the same time, as directed by the master. This is the order that is usually made when consolidation orders cannot for some reason be granted inasmuch as the avoidance of additional expense and multiplicity of actions can usually be accomplished in this way. Provision for such an order is set out in R. 229 and the same factors need to be considered as in an application for a consolidation order. Scheidl v. Southam Inc. (1981), 16 Alta. L.R. (2d) 158 (Q.B.), (reversed in result by C.A., but the proposition was not criticized, see Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd., supra, at 45). 7. Stay of Proceedings In Jardine Lloyd Thompson Canada Inc. v. Western Oil Sands Inc., 2006 ABQB 933, 2006 CarswellAlta 1750, 406 A.R. 23, 67 Alta. L.R. (4th) 165, Wittmann A.C.J.Q.B. had before him an application for a stay of proceedings “pending the outcome of related arbitration proceedings.” His Lordship reviewed the law, and concluded that he was bound by principles set forth in Alberta v. A.U.P.E. (1984), 53 A.R. 277 (Alta. C.A.), but that they are to be applied in a manner consistent with the efficient resolution of the disputes. He specifically found such an approach to be preferable to the stricter approach taken by Master Funduk in Bank of British Columbia v. Sitko (1986), 68 A.R. 65 (Alta. Q.B.). A.C.J. Wittmann said, at pp. 168–170: 9 The parties are agreed that this Court has jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings, that the remedy is discretionary and that it must be exercised in accordance with established principles. Those principles were described by Belzil J.A. in Alberta, Province of v. Alberta, Union Provincial Employees (1984), 53 A.R. 277 (C.A.) (“AUPE”), at paras. 9-10: The first and basic question to be addressed in such cases is whether the issues in the action sought to be stayed are substantially the same as those in the ‘test action’. If they are not, a stay will not be ordered … If the issues are substantially the same, a stay may and should be ordered if other tests are satisfied. Having thus concluded that the issues in the two proceedings are substantially the same, the remaining principles to be considered in determining whether this was a proper case for a stay are those set out by Scott, L.J., in St. Pierre v. South American Stores Ltd., [1935] All E.R. 408 (C.A.), at p.414:(I) a mere balance of convenience is not a sufficient ground for depriving a plaintiff of the advantages of prosecuting his action in English Court if it is otherwise properly brought. The right of access to the King's Court must not be lightly refused; (ii) in order to justify a stay two conditions must be satisfied, one positive and the other negative; (a) the defendant must satisfy the court that the continuance of the action would work an injustice because it would be oppressive, or vexatious to him, or would be an abuse of the powers of the court in some other way, and (b) the stay must not cause an injustice to the plaintiff. On both the burden of proof is on the defendant. 10 In Bank of British Columbia v. Sitko (1986), 68 A.R. 65 (Q.B.), Master Funduk considered AUPE and held, at paras.38-39: If an adjudication in the first action does not necessarily dispose of the issues in the second action it cannot be said there is a true duplication of proceedings in all respects. What is mandatory is that the issues be the same in both actions and that an adjudication in one action regardless of what that adjudication is, automatically disposes of the issues in the second action. 11 Consequently, Master Funduk was of the view that claims pleaded in the alternative are not appropriate for a stay. 12 A different approach was taken by the Ontario High Court in Boart Sweden Ab v. Nya Stromnes Ab., [1988] O.J. No. 2839 (H.C.). Boart concerned an action for breach of contract, as well as conspiracy to induce breach of contract and unlawful interference with economic relations arising out of the alleged breach of an exclusive distribution agreement. The parties to the agreement were bound by an arbitration clause, but the Ontario action added parties and causes of action that did not strictly arise out of the agreement itself. Campbell J. did not apply the test set out in AUPE. In fact, he cited no authority directly on the point but concluded at paras. 20-22 that it was appropriate to grant the stay. He said: The factual basis of all the issues in the Ontario action has to do with the conduct of the parties under the international agreement which is the subject of arbitration. To the extent that Boart Canada is an assignee of the rights of Boart Sweden under the international agreement it is bound by the arbitration agreement. It would be idle to proceed with the tort claims in Canada at the very same time that the arbitration proceeds in Sweden, even though the causes of action and the parties are not identical, when the factual basis of the tort claims is so tied up together with the matters being decided in the arbitration and when there is an obvious overlap between the witnesses required for the different proceedings in the two different countries. Campbell J. further noted, at para. 28: The matters in dispute in the Ontario action are inextricably bound up with the matter which the parties agreed to arbitrate. It would be mischievous to continue to litigate, pending arbitration, matters which depend so much on the facts which form the basis of the arbitration. Justice Wittmann then reviewed a number of cases, and concluded, at p. 175: In my view, the approach taken by the Court in Boart…is preferable to the more strict approach exemplified by Master Funduk's application of the AUPE test in Sitko. This Court is bound by the decision in AUPE, and must apply the test therein. However, it is appropriate to apply that test in the context and spirit of the authorities cited above, which suggest that the Court must have a view to the efficient resolution of disputes and the efficient management of the resources of the Court and the parties. Stratton J.A. has said: This rule seems to be simply a codification of the “just and reasonable rules” set out in Edmeades v. Thames Board Mills Ltd., [1969] 2 Q.B. 67, at 71 where Lord Denning, M.R., stated: I do not think legislation is necessary. This court has ample jurisdiction to grant a stay whenever it is just and reasonable so to do. As pointed out by the respondent, this concept was specifically adopted in Lane v. Willis, [1972] 1 A11 E.R. 430 (C.A.), wherein Davies, L.J., said: I for myself adhere firmly to the opinion which this court expressed in Edmeade's case, namely, that in an appropriate case, given the right circumstances, this court has the jurisdiction to make that order (for a stay). Vanbrabant v. Alberta (Minister of Education) (1989), 102 A.R. 77 at 79 (C.A.). 8. Common Question Rule 229 speaks in terms of a common question of law and does not require that all questions of law or fact in both actions must be common. Vanbrabant v. Alberta (Minister of Education) (1989), 102 A.R. 77 at 79 (C.A.). And Mr. Justice Gallant has said: Even if the fact that the application is being made at a late stage of the proceedings and the fact that the parties in the two actions are not the same are factors mitigating against granting a consolidation order, those factors do not militate against an order that these matters be heard consecutively. The jurisprudence on this issue establishes that where there are common issues to be tried, a Rule 229 order providing that the matters be heard consecutively is appropriate even where the matters are at an advanced stage in the proceedings … or where the parties are not the same… Nevertheless, it does not suffice that there are no contra-indicators to an order for the matters to be tried consecutively. It is clear that Rule 229 requires that before such an order be granted, there must be a common question of law or fact, or some other reason to justify the granting of such an order. Alberta v. Alberta (Labour Relations Board) (1997), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 171 at 177-78 (Q.B.). And Madam Justice Kent has said: In Thames Steel Construction Ltd. v. Portman et al. (1980), 28 O.R. (2d) 445 (H.C.), Griffiths, J., says at 453: In my view, where the alternative claims arise out of the same transaction or series of transactions and involve a common question of fact or law, then the governing principle in determining whether joinder should be allowed is … the balance of convenience. In Thames, supra, the balance of convenience test is articulated at 453 as: “whether the expense and delay that would be caused by compelling the Plaintiff to bring separate actions against the proposed Defendant would be greatly out of proportion to the inconvenience, expense or embarrassment which that Defendant would be put if the actions were tried together.”Grebely (Andy & Jean) Holdings Ltd. v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. of Canada ((2000),), 383 A.R. 296 at 299-300 ((Q.B.)). 9. Miscellaneous Effects of Consolidation If two actions are consolidated, then they become one action and applications under R. 4.31 must relate to the new single action, not just one of the old actions. In my view, the order consolidates the actions so that there is now only one action. The order does not provide the actions be tried together but that they be consolidated and proceed as one action. In my view, it is not possible to split an action for the purpose of an application under Rule 243. Wal-Mar Construction v. Guarantee Co. of North America (1981), 33 A.R. 88 at 90 (Master). The matter cannot be set down for trial until all items (e.g., undertakings etc.) in the actions that were consolidated are satisfied. As I have ordered that the two actions be tried together both actions must be ready for trial before they can be set down for trial. Because of the outstanding undertakings in the second action such a finding is not possible. Arnold v. Larkin (1984), 55 A.R. 125 at 128 (Master). 10. Notice of Application See Rule 6.3 and the annotations thereunder [particularly the annotation dealing with Sitko v. Hartum (2004), 43 Alta. L.R. (4th) 333 (Q.B.).
